newsitem.title: USA: Calif. hydropower outlook improves amid new snow.
newsitem.headline: Calif. hydropower outlook improves amid new snow.

text.p: The outlook for California hydroelectric generation continued to improve, with storms this week replacing some of the lower-elevation snowpack lost during recent warm rainfall, industry experts said Thursday.
"If we had no more rain between now and the end of the water year (September 30) we would still finish above normal," a California utility hydrologist said.

During January-October of last year, hydroelectricity accounted for 39 percent of total California power generation, compared with 41 percent in the same 1995 period, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

As of Thursday, snowpack in the southern Sierra Nevada mountains stood near 190 percent of normal, while the central Sierra total was close to 150 percent and the northern Sierra was above 100 percent, the U.S. Natural Resources Conservation Service reported.
Reservoirs are described as too full for this early in the season, with most still being drawn down to accomodate future rainfall.
Operators of federal dams said outflows continue to outstrip inflows at most projects as space is cleared for flood protection.
Some spillage was reported, but U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (BuRec) officials said as much water as possible was being run through turbines rather than spillways.
"We are generating as much as we can," said Bill Hagbery, manager of power operations at BuRec's central California projects.
Dam operations are also being stepped up to protect the facilities themselves and because of water entitlements.
Under contracts with farmers established when the dam systems were built early this century, utilities are required at most projects to release all the water received in a given year.
Hydroelectric projects also face difficulties from the recent heavy flows, which damaged some dam facings, intake stations and gauging instruments.
In addition, if reservoirs freeze when they are full, docks and other facilties could be damaged, said one dam operator.
